title: Most Common Values in a Search Tree
statement:
You get the root of a binary search tree that may hold repeated values. Every value in a node's left subtree is less than or equal to the node's value, and every value in its right subtree is greater than or equal to it.

Return every value that occurs the greatest number of times in the tree. If several values tie for the top count, return all of them, in any order.

examples.why: 7 appears three times, 3 twice and 5 once.
Each of the three values appears twice, so all of them tie for the top.
A single node is its own most common value.

constraints: The tree is a valid search tree as described above
hints: Counting with a hash map works for any tree. What does the search-tree order give you on top of that?
An in-order walk visits the values in sorted order, so equal values come out next to each other.
Walk in order and keep the previous value, the length of the current streak of equal values and the best streak so far. A longer streak resets the answer list; an equal one adds to it.

explain.intuition:
In a search tree, an in-order walk (left, node, right) produces the values in sorted order. Sorted order puts every copy of a value in one contiguous streak. So counting occurrences becomes counting streak lengths, which needs no map at all, just the previous value and the current streak length.

This is the same trick as finding the most repeated item in a sorted list. The tree only changes how you get the sorted order.
steps: Walk the tree in order (iteratively with a stack, or recursively).
For each value: if it equals the previous value, increase streak; otherwise set streak = 1. Remember it as the previous value.
If streak > best, set best = streak and reset the answer to just this value.
Else if streak == best, append this value to the answer.
Return the answer after the walk.
pitfalls: Comparing only a node with its children. Copies of a value can be far apart in the tree, like the two 4s in the second example.
Returning just one value when several tie for the top count.
Starting previous at 0 or another real value. If the first value is 0 it would be wrongly counted as a streak of 2. Use a separate flag or null.

complexity.space: O(h) for the walk, plus the output

solutions.title: Count with a hash map
solutions.idea: Visit every node, count values in a map, then return the values whose count equals the maximum.

solutions.title: In-order walk with a running streak
solutions.idea: In-order order is sorted, so equal values are consecutive. Track the current streak and the best one; no map needed.

followups: Can you do it with O(1) extra space, not even a stack? (Look up Morris traversal.)
The tree changes often and you are asked for the modes after each insert. What would you store?
